title: Carved birch egg ladle
subtitle: A deep-bowled ladle for lifting eggs from boiling water
excerpt: A birch ladle with a deep hemispherical bowl sized for a hen's egg. Green birch, axe rough-out, hook knife deep bowl, sloyd finish. The long handle keeps hands away from boiling water and the deep bowl prevents rolling.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for tool sequences; Museum of English Rural Life open-access photographs of rural kitchen wooden ladles, 19th century.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freshly felled or recently riven wood, still high in moisture content. Carves easily under hand tools.
The rough-shaped piece of wood from which the finished item is carved.
A curved-bladed knife for hollowing the bowl of a spoon or kuksa. Three radius sizes: small, medium, and large for the everyday bowl; deep for ladles and kuksas.
A leather strap charged with abrasive compound, used to maintain a sharp edge between honings.

content.text: An egg ladle is a deep-bowled spoon sized to cradle a hen's egg. The bowl needs to be at least 4 cm deep and 5 cm across at the rim so the egg sits steady rather than rolling. The handle is 22 cm long with a slight offset at the bowl shoulder so the ladle sits flat when resting on a pan rim. This is an intermediate project because the deep bowl requires careful hook-knife control; the blank preparation and handle work are the same as the beginner eating spoon.
This project wants
green wood
. Birch carves easily and dries food-safe. The
blank
starts at 30 cm long and 7 cm wide. A quarter-section split from a birch log, with the handle on the outer face, gives the cleanest grain run.
Before you start cutting.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: push cuts (blade away from body) and thumb-pivot cuts are the default. Pull cuts only with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc unable to reach anything vital.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one. The dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Workspace: stable seat, good light, no children or pets within arm-and-blade reach.
Wood

Birch: strong in thin sections, food-safe, sourced from windfall or tree-surgeon off-cuts. The bowl walls will be 6 to 8 mm thick at the rim and thicker at the base. Birch handles this wall-to-depth ratio reliably. Sycamore also works. Ash is less suited here: the shorter grain at the bowl shoulder in a deep profile is a weak point in ash.
Tools
Carving axe: rough-out the blank silhouette.
Sloyd knife: profile the handle and the outside of the bowl.
Hook knife, medium: start the bowl hollow.
Hook knife, deep (optional): for the final 10 mm of depth, a deep-radius hook knife reaches the bottom without the blade tip touching the rim.
Leather strop: strop every fifteen minutes.
Raw linseed oil: food-safe finish with a two-week cure.
Workspace
The same low-stool setup as an eating spoon. The blank is slightly longer and requires more axe work at the rough-out stage; extra room around the chopping block helps.
Method
Step 1: Mark the offset

The bowl shoulder sits 5 mm lower than the handle plane on a ladle. This offset means the ladle rests flat on a pan rim without the bowl tipping forward. Mark the offset line on the side of the blank before axe work begins.
Step 2: Axe the outline

Axe the plan view silhouette. The bowl section will be deeper than a standard spoon blank, which means more material to remove at the rough-out. Take your time; do not try to axe past the marked line.
Step 3: Profile the handle and bowl exterior

Use the sloyd knife to profile the handle cross-section and to shape the outside of the bowl. The outside of the bowl is a dome: it curves smoothly from the rim down to the base with no flat spots. Push cuts from the rim toward the centre on the bowl back, reversing direction where the grain shifts.
Step 4: Hollow the bowl
Begin with the medium
hook knife

. Work from the rim inward in circular strokes, removing a little depth on each pass. Check depth with a pencil marked at 4 cm: when the pencil drops to the mark in the centre, the depth is right. Wall thickness should be 6 to 8 mm at the rim and 10 mm at the base.

For the last 10 mm of depth, switch to the deep hook knife if available. The deeper radius reaches the bottom of the bowl without the blade tip scraping the rim wall. If using only the medium hook knife, work at a steep angle and in short strokes, checking repeatedly that the rim walls remain even.
The grain at the base of a deep bowl runs across the cut direction on every stroke. Short, sharp cuts with a well-stropped edge prevent tearing.
Strop
the hook knife every ten minutes on the deep-bowl work.
Step 5: The pan-rim groove

Some egg ladles have a shallow groove on the underside of the handle near the bowl shoulder, 10 mm back from the bowl. This groove hooks over the pan rim and stops the ladle sliding in. Mark the groove and use the tip of the sloyd knife to score the groove walls, then remove a chip between them. The groove is 3 mm deep and 5 mm wide. This is optional but useful.
Finishing

Dry for one week before oiling. Apply raw linseed oil to all surfaces including the bowl interior. Let the interior soak for an hour; the deep bowl holds more oil than a flat surface and the wood at the base is thicker and takes longer to saturate. Wipe the surplus and cure for two weeks. The cure time for a deep bowl interior is the same two weeks as for a shallow bowl: the critical factor is surface oxidation, not thickness.
Variations
Widen the bowl to 7 cm across to fit a large hen's egg or a duck egg.
Drill a 10 mm hole in the handle tip for hanging storage.
A pair makes a useful serving set: one deep-bowled egg ladle and one wide-bowled serving spoon from entry 01 of this batch.
Care

The deep bowl accumulates water after washing. After hand-washing, tip the ladle upside-down on the drying rack. Water left standing in the bowl overnight can penetrate any crack in the finish. Re-oil when the wood looks dry, once or twice a year under normal use.

attrs.symptom: The bowl walls are thinner on one side
attrs.cause: The hook knife drifted off the circular track.
attrs.fix: Mark the planned oval with a pencil before hollowing and check the mark against the cut after every three strokes.

attrs.symptom: The hook knife is tearing the grain at the base of the bowl
attrs.cause: The edge has dulled or the cut is going against the grain.
attrs.fix: Strop the knife. Then try a different stroke direction: rotate the spoon and approach the same spot from the opposite side.

attrs.symptom: The offset at the bowl shoulder is not even
attrs.cause: The cut was made freehand without checking the marked line on both sides.
attrs.fix: Mark the offset on both sides of the blank and use both marks as a guide. The offset should be the same depth on both sides of the handle.
